The support measures in Article 62 attach to status as an SME, including start-ups, rather than to headcount alone, and they continue for as long as that status is held; the Act does not itself fix the size thresholds that determine it. Those measures consist of priority access to the AI regulatory sandboxes for SMEs having a registered office or a branch in the Union that meet the eligibility conditions and selection criteria, tailored awareness raising and training activities, dedicated communication channels for advice and queries, and facilitated participation in standardisation. Under Article 62(2), fees for conformity assessment are reduced proportionately to size, market size and other relevant indicators, so that relief tapers with growth instead of ending abruptly. No substantive duty changes with size in any event, since the obligations of a provider or deployer of a high-risk AI system apply irrespective of undertaking size.

question: We're a GPAI provider that fine-tuned another model with 35% of the base model's compute. Did we become the new provider?
answer: Yes, at 35% of the base model's compute the fine-tuning provider becomes the provider of the resulting model, because additional training compute exceeding one third of the base model's cumulative training compute is treated as making the modifier a new provider under Article 25, which treats a third party that makes a substantial modification to an already marketed model as a provider bearing the provider obligations. As the new provider, the obligations under Article 53 apply to the modified model, namely technical documentation of the model including its training, testing and evaluation results with at least the elements of Annex XI, information and documentation for downstream providers integrating the model containing at least the elements of Annex XII, a policy to comply with Union copyright law including reservations of rights, and a sufficiently detailed publicly available summary of the training content. In practice these duties attach to the modification itself, and the original provider remains responsible for the base model and must supply the information and technical access the downstream provider needs. If the modified model's cumulative training compute exceeds 10^25 floating point operations it is presumed under Article 51 to have high impact capabilities and is classified as a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk, triggering the four additional Article 55 duties of state-of-the-art model evaluation with adversarial testing, assessment and mitigation of systemic risks at Union level, reporting of serious incidents to the AI Office without undue delay, and adequate cybersecurity protection for the model and its physical infrastructure.

question: We built an internal AI for our own HR use — never released externally. Are we a provider or just a deployer?
answer: Putting an AI system into service for one's own internal use makes the organisation a provider, not merely a deployer, since provider status attaches to development and putting into service under one's own name irrespective of whether the system is ever placed on the market externally, and Article 25 confirms that a deployer that puts its own name or trademark on a system or substantially modifies it assumes all provider obligations. The organisation therefore carries provider duties and, because it also uses the system in its own operations, the deployer duties under Article 26 to use the system in accordance with the instructions for use, assign human oversight to competent and trained natural persons, monitor operation, and keep the automatically generated logs for at least six months. Article 26(7) additionally requires an employer deploying a high-risk AI system at the workplace to inform workers' representatives and the affected workers before putting it into service or using it. Both roles also trigger the Article 4 duty to ensure a sufficient level of AI literacy among staff and other persons operating the system.

question: A non-EU company sells AI to EU customers but has no EU establishment. Who is liable on the EU side?
answer: The provider itself remains liable, and it must appoint an authorised representative established in the Union by written mandate before making a high-risk AI system available on the Union market, since providers established in third countries fall within the Regulation's scope when they place systems on the EU market (Article 22). That authorised representative verifies that the EU declaration of conformity and the technical documentation have been drawn up, keeps them at the disposal of competent authorities for 10 years, provides information and log access on reasoned request, cooperates with market surveillance authorities, and may be addressed in addition to or instead of the provider on all compliance issues (Article 22). If the authorised representative considers the provider to be acting contrary to its obligations, it must terminate the mandate and immediately inform the relevant market surveillance authority (Article 22). Any EU-side operator that makes the system available on the market bears its own distributor duties to verify the CE marking, the EU declaration of conformity and the instructions for use (Article 24), and any distributor, importer or deployer that puts its own name or trademark on the system or substantially modifies it becomes a provider and assumes the full provider obligations (Article 25).

question: An importer rebrands a high-risk AI under its own name before selling it on. Do they become the provider?
answer: Yes. Under Article 25(1), a distributor, importer, deployer or other third party is deemed to be the provider of a high-risk AI system, and takes on the provider obligations in Article 16, in any of three cases. First, if it puts its name or trademark on a high-risk AI system already placed on the market (Article 25(1)(a)). Second, if it makes a substantial modification to a high-risk AI system that remains high-risk (Article 25(1)(b)). Third, if it modifies the intended purpose of an AI system, including a general-purpose AI system, so that it becomes high-risk (Article 25(1)(c)). In each of these three cases the operator assumes the provider obligations in Article 16, and the initial provider is no longer considered the provider of that specific system under Article 25(2).

question: Our SaaS lets enterprise customers configure a CV-screening AI for their hiring. Are we the provider or are they?
answer: The SaaS company is the provider, and the enterprise customer is normally the deployer. The provider is the entity that develops the CV-screening system and places it on the market or puts it into service under its own name or trademark, and it bears the Article 16 provider obligations to ensure the system meets the high-risk requirements, operate a quality management system, and keep the technical documentation. An enterprise customer that merely configures the system within the intended purpose set by the provider remains a deployer under Article 26, obliged to use the system in accordance with the instructions for use, assign human oversight to competent and trained natural persons, and monitor its operation. That customer becomes a provider itself, assuming the full Article 16 obligations, in the circumstances set out in Article 25, namely putting its own name or trademark on the system, making a substantial modification to it, or modifying its intended purpose so that it becomes high-risk.

question: We resell a CE-marked high-risk biometric AI without modifying it. What are our obligations as distributor?
answer: Reselling without modification keeps the entity a distributor, so Article 24 governs and the provider requirements do not attach. Before making the high-risk AI system available on the market, the distributor must verify that it bears the required CE marking, that it is accompanied by a copy of the EU declaration of conformity and the instructions for use, and that the provider and importer have complied with their respective obligations. Where the distributor considers, or has reason to consider on the basis of information in its possession, that the system is not in conformity, it must not make it available until conformity is restored, and it must inform the provider or importer where the system presents a risk; it must also ensure that storage or transport conditions under its responsibility do not jeopardise compliance, take or ensure corrective action, withdrawal or recall for systems already made available, and immediately inform the provider or importer and the competent authorities where such a system presents a risk. On a reasoned request the distributor must supply competent authorities with all information and documentation on those actions and must cooperate with them in any action taken to reduce or mitigate the risk, and it would assume provider obligations under Article 25 only if it put its name or trademark on the system, made a substantial modification, or changed its intended purpose.

question: If my chatbot is also a high-risk medical-triage AI, does Article 13 transparency or Article 50 chatbot-disclosure apply?
answer: Both apply, cumulatively. Article 13 requires the high-risk system to be designed for sufficiently transparent operation so deployers can interpret its output and use it appropriately, and to be accompanied by instructions for use stating provider identity and contact details, intended purpose, capabilities and limitations including accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity metrics, foreseeable circumstances that may lead to risks to health, safety or fundamental rights, human oversight measures, pre-determined changes, expected lifetime and necessary maintenance, and log-interpretation mechanisms. Article 50(1) separately requires the provider to design a system intended to interact directly with natural persons so that those persons are informed they are interacting with an AI system, unless that is obvious to a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person, and Article 50(5) requires that information to be given clearly and distinguishably at the latest at the first interaction. Article 50(6) confirms these transparency duties do not affect the Chapter III high-risk requirements, so the deployer-facing chain under Article 13 and the end-user-facing disclosure under Article 50 must both be satisfied.

question: Our Annex IV technical documentation contains trade secrets. Article 78 says authorities must keep them confidential — can we refuse to share them under Article 11?
answer: No. Article 78(1) binds the Commission, market surveillance authorities, notified bodies and any other person involved in applying the Regulation to protect intellectual property rights, confidential business information and trade secrets including source code, but it constrains how those authorities handle the documentation, not whether a provider must produce it. Article 11(1) requires the technical documentation to be drawn up before the high-risk AI system is placed on the market, kept up to date, and framed so that national competent authorities and notified bodies receive the Annex IV elements in a clear and comprehensive form to assess compliance, and Annex IV fixes that minimum content including the design specifications and general logic of the algorithms, the system architecture and the computational resources used to develop, train, test and validate the system. Article 74(12) reinforces this by granting market surveillance authorities full access to the documentation and to the training, validation and testing data sets, limited to what is necessary to fulfil their tasks. The protection available is therefore confidentiality in the authority's hands under Article 78, reinforced by the Article 78(2) duty to request only strictly necessary data, to apply adequate cybersecurity measures and to delete data once no longer needed, not a right to withhold.

question: A FRIA under Article 27 and a conformity assessment under Article 43 cover overlapping fundamental-rights checks. Can we skip one?
answer: No, neither obligation can be substituted for the other. The conformity assessment under Article 43 is a provider duty discharged before placing on the market, following the internal control procedure of Annex VI or the quality management system and technical documentation assessment with notified body involvement under Annex VII, and it demonstrates conformity of the system itself with the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements. The fundamental rights impact assessment under Article 27 is a separate deployer duty owed before first use by bodies governed by public law, private entities providing public services, and deployers of the Annex III point 5(b) creditworthiness and point 5(c) life and health insurance systems, covering the deployer's own processes, the period and frequency of use, the categories of persons affected, the specific risks of harm, human oversight measures, and internal governance and complaint mechanisms, with the sole exclusion being systems intended for the Annex III point 2 critical infrastructure area. The only permitted economies are internal to Article 27 itself: under Article 27(2) a deployer may rely in similar cases on previously conducted fundamental rights impact assessments or on existing impact assessments carried out by the provider, and under Article 27(4) where obligations are already met through a data protection impact assessment the fundamental rights impact assessment complements rather than duplicates it.

question: Article 13 says transparency, Article 86 says right to explanation. Aren't they the same thing?
answer: No, they are distinct obligations owed to different persons at different points in the lifecycle. Article 13 is a design and documentation requirement on the provider: the high-risk AI system must be sufficiently transparent to enable deployers to interpret its output and use it appropriately, and it must be accompanied by instructions for use that are concise, complete, correct and clear, covering the intended purpose, the level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity against which it was tested, known or foreseeable circumstances that may lead to risks to health, safety or fundamental rights, and information enabling deployers to interpret the output. Article 86 instead confers an individual right exercisable after the fact against the deployer, allowing any affected person subject to a decision taken on the basis of output from an Annex III high-risk AI system, other than the critical infrastructure systems in point 2, that produces legal effects or similarly significantly adversely affects their health, safety or fundamental rights, to obtain clear and meaningful explanations of the role of the AI system in the decision-making procedure and the main elements of the decision, though that right does not apply where Union or national law provides exceptions or where the right is already provided for under Union law. In short, Article 13 gives the deployer generic ex ante system knowledge, while Article 86 gives the affected person an ex post explanation of one specific decision.

question: Is biometric categorization for age detection in a retail store prohibited under Article 5(1)(g)?
answer: Biometric categorisation for age detection in a retail store is not a prohibited practice, because Article 5 bars biometric categorisation only where it deduces or infers race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation, and age is not among those attributes. Such a system falls instead under Annex III, point 1(b), which lists AI systems intended to be used for biometric categorisation according to sensitive or protected attributes based on the inference of those attributes, placing it in the high-risk tier rather than the prohibited one. It would become a prohibited practice under Article 5 only if it exploited vulnerabilities of a natural person or group due to their age, with the objective or effect of materially distorting their behaviour in a manner that causes or is reasonably likely to cause significant harm.

question: We use emotion recognition in a medical-device AI to monitor pain in non-verbal patients. Is that prohibited?
answer: Emotion recognition is not categorically prohibited under the AI Act; the prohibition in Article 5 only applies in workplaces and educational institutions, with a narrow medical/safety exception. Elsewhere the system is high-risk under Annex III.1(c) and triggers Article 50(3) transparency duties toward exposed persons.

question: Is real-time RBI in public spaces prohibited for police investigating ongoing terrorist attacks?
answer: Real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement purposes is prohibited under Article 5, but not in this scenario: Article 5(1)(h)(ii) exempts use that is strictly necessary for the prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to the life or physical safety of natural persons or a genuine and present or genuine and foreseeable threat of a terrorist attack, which an ongoing terrorist attack satisfies. Article 5(1)(h)(iii) separately permits such use for the localisation or identification of a person suspected of an offence listed in terrorism among them, punishable in the Member State concerned by a custodial sentence or detention order of at least four years. The exemption is strictly construed and is confined to what is strictly necessary for that objective, so blanket or continuous deployment beyond the operational response to the attack falls back within the prohibition. Article 5(1)(h) is without prejudice to Article 9 of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 for the processing of biometric data for purposes other than law enforcement.

question: We scrape facial images from publicly available CCTV footage to build a recognition database. Is that prohibited?
answer: Prohibited, where the facial images are collected through untargeted scraping. Article 5(1)(e) prohibits the placing on the market, the putting into service for this specific purpose, or the use of AI systems that create or expand facial recognition databases through the untargeted scraping of facial images from the internet or CCTV footage, and the public availability of the CCTV footage does not remove the practice from that prohibition. The prohibition applies irrespective of whether the resulting database is temporary, centralised or decentralised, and it operates without prejudice to prohibitions arising where an AI practice infringes other Union law under Article 5(8). Only targeted collection directed at specifically identified individuals, rather than untargeted scraping of facial images at scale, falls outside Article 5(1)(e).

question: We use AI to score creditworthiness on a 1-10 scale used internally only — not shared, not affecting public services. Is that social scoring?
answer: No, not on those facts. Article 5 prohibits social scoring only where an AI system evaluates or classifies natural persons over a period of time on the basis of their social behaviour or known, inferred or predicted personal or personality characteristics, and the resulting score causes detrimental or unfavourable treatment in social contexts unrelated to the context in which the data was originally generated or collected, or treatment that is unjustified or disproportionate to that social behaviour or its gravity. A score derived from financial data and used solely to assess credit remains within the context in which the data was generated and is proportionate to that purpose, so neither limb is engaged; the internal-only, unpublished character of the score is not what decides this, and a system that pulled in unrelated social behaviour data or drove treatment outside the credit context could still fall within the prohibition. Creditworthiness evaluation and credit scoring of natural persons is instead a listed use case under Annex III, which makes the system high-risk rather than a prohibited practice, save where it is used to detect financial fraud.

question: Our GPAI is open-weights but we trained at exactly 1×10²⁵ FLOPs. Do we still get the Article 53(2) open-weights carve-out?
answer: Yes, on those facts the Article 53(2) carve-out is available, because Article 51(2) presumes high impact capabilities only where cumulative training compute is greater than 10^25 floating point operations, and a model trained at exactly 1×10^25 FLOPs does not cross that threshold. The carve-out therefore removes the Article 53(1)(a) Annex XI technical documentation duty and the Article 53(1)(b) Annex XII downstream information duty, provided the licence genuinely allows access, usage, modification and distribution and the parameters, including the weights, the model architecture information and the model usage information, are made publicly available. It remains conditional: the Commission may still classify the model as a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk under Article 51(1)(b) on the Annex XIII criteria, and any such designation extinguishes the exception and brings the full Article 53 obligations plus the four Article 55 duties of model evaluation with adversarial testing, systemic risk assessment and mitigation, serious incident reporting to the AI Office, and cybersecurity protection of the model and its physical infrastructure. Regardless of the open-source licence, the Article 53(1)(c) copyright policy and the Article 53(1)(d) publicly available sufficiently detailed training content summary continue to apply.

question: We fine-tune a third-party GPAI with 30% of the base compute. Are we now the provider?
answer: No. Additional training compute at 30% of the base model's compute falls below the one-third benchmark that marks a modification as substantial enough to make the downstream modifier a new provider, so responsibility for the general-purpose AI model remains with the original provider, consistent with Article 25, under which a third party is treated as a provider and assumes the provider obligations where it puts its name or trademark on the system or makes a substantial modification. Had the threshold been crossed, the Article 53 obligations would attach in respect of the modification, namely technical documentation of the model per Annex XI, the information and documentation for downstream providers integrating the model per Annex XII, a copyright policy including respect for rights reservations, and a sufficiently detailed publicly available summary of the training content. Where the resulting model has high impact capabilities, presumed under Article 51 when cumulative training compute exceeds 10^25 floating point operations, the Article 55 systemic risk duties of model evaluation with adversarial testing, systemic risk assessment and mitigation, serious incident reporting to the AI Office, and adequate cybersecurity protection would apply in addition.

question: Does the AI Act require GPAI providers to disclose training data sources?
answer: Yes, in summary form. Article 53(1)(d) requires every provider of a general-purpose AI model to draw up and make publicly available a sufficiently detailed summary about the content used for training the model, following the template provided by the AI Office, which covers public datasets, scraped web content, user data, synthetic data and licensed content. This duty is not a disclosure of exhaustive source lists, and it sits alongside the Article 53(1)(a) technical documentation of the training and testing process containing at least the Annex XI information for the AI Office and national competent authorities on request, the Article 53(1)(b) information for downstream providers containing at least the Annex XII elements including a training-data summary, and the Article 53(1)(c) copyright policy. The Article 53(2) exemption for models released under a free and open-source licence with publicly available parameters removes only the points (a) and (b) documentation duties, and it does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk, so the public training-content summary is owed by all providers.

question: If we use a GPAI as a component in our high-risk AI, do GPAI obligations transfer to us?
answer: No, the Article 53 obligations remain with the provider of the general-purpose AI model and do not transfer to a downstream provider merely because the model is integrated as a component into a high-risk AI system. Article 53(1) places on the model provider the duties to draw up Annex XI technical documentation covering the training, testing and evaluation of the model, to make available to providers integrating the model the Annex XII downstream information on its capabilities, limitations and intended tasks, to put in place a copyright policy, and to publish a sufficiently detailed summary of the training content, with Article 53(2) exempting only points (a) and (b) for free and open-source releases with publicly available parameters and never for models with systemic risk. The practical effect for the integrator is entitlement to that Article 53(1)(b) information, which must enable it to understand the model and comply with its own obligations under the Regulation. The position changes only where the integrator itself becomes the provider of a general-purpose AI model, for instance by modifying or fine-tuning it beyond one third of the original training compute, in which case Article 53 applies to it directly and, if the model crosses the Article 51 high-impact capability threshold of 10^25 floating point operations, the Article 55 duties of model evaluation including adversarial testing, systemic risk assessment and mitigation, serious incident reporting to the AI Office, and cybersecurity protection of the model and its physical infrastructure apply on top.

question: We're a GPAI provider with no EU establishment. Can we appoint our European customer as our authorised representative?
answer: Yes, provided that customer is established in the Union and accepts the appointment by written mandate, because Article 22 requires a provider established in a third country to appoint by written mandate an authorised representative established in the Union and attaches no independence or non-affiliation condition to who may be appointed. The mandate must empower the representative to verify that the technical documentation and the EU declaration of conformity have been drawn up and that the conformity assessment has been carried out, to keep that documentation available to competent authorities for 10 years, to supply information and cooperate on reasoned request, and to comply with the applicable registration obligations, and the provider must enable it to perform those tasks. Practical caution is warranted because Article 22 also obliges the authorised representative to terminate the mandate and immediately inform the relevant market surveillance authority where it considers the provider to be acting contrary to its obligations, a duty the customer must be free to exercise against its own supplier. If that same entity puts its name or trademark on the system or makes a substantial modification, Article 25 makes it a provider in its own right and it assumes the full provider obligations rather than the representative role.

question: Our medical-device AI is already CE-marked under MDR. Do we still need a separate AI Act conformity assessment?
answer: No separate AI Act conformity assessment is required, but the AI Act requirements must be added into the existing MDR procedure. Under Article 43(3), for high-risk AI systems covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Section A of Annex I, which includes Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on medical devices, the provider follows the relevant sectoral conformity assessment procedure, and the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements apply to the system and form part of that assessment. In practice the notified body already notified under the medical devices regime controls conformity with those requirements, provided its compliance with the applicable notified-body requirements has been assessed in the context of that notification, so one single procedure and one CE marking cover both regimes. Article 43(4) then requires a new conformity assessment in the event of a substantial modification, although pre-determined changes documented in the technical documentation at the time of the initial assessment do not count as such.Practically, this means folding the Chapter III, Section 2 evidence into the operator's existing technical documentation and quality management system and raising it with the operator's current notified body at the next MDR surveillance or recertification cycle, rather than opening a second, parallel assessment track.

question: Does our existing GDPR Article 35 DPIA satisfy the Article 27 FRIA requirement?
answer: No. A data protection impact assessment under Article 35 of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 does not discharge the fundamental rights impact assessment, because Article 27(4) provides that where obligations are already met through that data protection impact assessment, the fundamental rights impact assessment complements it rather than replaces it. The deployer must still cover the elements Article 27(1) requires, namely a description of the processes in which the high-risk AI system will be used in line with its intended purpose, the period and frequency of intended use, the categories of natural persons and groups likely to be affected, the specific risks of harm to them, the implementation of human oversight measures according to the instructions for use, and the measures to be taken if those risks materialise, including internal governance arrangements and complaint mechanisms. Under Article 27(2) the obligation attaches to first use, and existing impact assessments may be relied on in similar cases, with an update required whenever any element changes or ceases to be up to date. Article 27(3) then requires the deployer to notify the market surveillance authority of the results using the template the AI Office develops under Article 27(5).

question: Our high-risk AI provides cybersecurity for critical infrastructure. We already report incidents under NIS2. Do AI Act incident-reporting obligations still apply?
answer: Yes, the AI Act's incident obligations continue to apply cumulatively, because compliance with NIS2 does not displace them. Article 26(5) requires deployers of high-risk AI systems to monitor operation on the basis of the instructions for use, to inform the provider in accordance with Article 72, and, where there is reason to consider that use in accordance with the instructions may result in the system presenting a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1), to inform the provider or distributor and the relevant market surveillance authority without undue delay and suspend use; where a serious incident is identified, the deployer must immediately inform first the provider, then the importer or distributor and the relevant market surveillance authorities, with Article 73 applying mutatis mutandis if the provider cannot be reached. The only qualifications Article 26(5) admits are the exclusion of sensitive operational data of deployers that are law enforcement authorities and the deemed fulfilment of the monitoring duty for deployers that are financial institutions complying with internal governance rules under Union financial services law; no equivalent relief exists for entities reporting under other Union cybersecurity law. Article 26(3) confirms that these deployer duties operate without prejudice to other obligations under Union or national law, so the two reporting regimes must be satisfied in parallel.

question: Which regulator do we register with under the AI Act side?
answer: No national regulator. Registration under Article 49 is made directly in the EU database established and managed by the Commission under Article 71, and providers of Annex III high-risk AI systems (or their authorised representative) must register themselves and the system there before placing it on the market or putting it into service, as required by Article 16 among the provider obligations. The same EU database registration applies under Article 49(2) where the provider has concluded, under the Article 6(3) derogation, that its Annex III system is not high-risk. Two carve-outs from the EU database route exist: high-risk AI systems in point 2 of Annex III (critical infrastructure) are registered at national level under Article 49(5), and systems under points 1, 6 and 7 of Annex III are entered in a secure non-public section of the database accessible only to the Commission and the national authorities referred to in Article 74(8).

question: Does our DPO's existing GDPR Art. 35 DPIA cover the AI Act obligations too, or do we still need the FRIA?
answer: A GDPR Article 35 data protection impact assessment does not discharge the fundamental rights impact assessment obligation. Where an obligation under Article 27 is already met through the data protection impact assessment conducted pursuant to Article 35 of Regulation (EU) 2016/679, Article 27(4) provides that the fundamental rights impact assessment complements that assessment rather than being replaced by it, so the existing work can be reused for the overlapping elements but the remaining Article 27(1) elements must still be produced. Those elements are a description of the deployer's processes in which the high-risk AI system will be used in line with its intended purpose, the period and frequency of intended use, the categories of natural persons and groups likely to be affected, the specific risks of harm to them taking account of the provider information under Article 13, the implementation of human oversight measures per the instructions for use, and the measures to be taken if those risks materialise including internal governance arrangements and complaint mechanisms. The fundamental rights impact assessment is also subject to duties the data protection impact assessment has no equivalent of, namely notification of its results to the market surveillance authority using the AI Office template under Article 27(3) and (5), and it is owed only by deployers that are bodies governed by public law or private entities providing public services, and deployers of the Annex III point 5(b) creditworthiness or credit scoring systems and point 5(c) life and health insurance risk assessment and pricing systems, with high-risk AI systems intended for the Annex III point 2 critical infrastructure area excluded.

question: What's the AI Act window then?
answer: For general-purpose AI models placed on the market from 2 August 2025 onwards, the Article 53 obligations apply immediately, while models already placed on the market before that date are grandfathered until 2 August 2027. Article 53(1)(d) requires every provider of a general-purpose AI model to draw up and make publicly available a sufficiently detailed summary of the content used for training, following the template the Commission adopted on 24 July 2025 and covering public datasets, scraped web content, user data, synthetic data and licensed content. That publication duty and the Article 53(1)(c) copyright policy, which requires state-of-the-art identification of rights reservations, bind all providers, including free and open-source releases. Only the Article 53(1)(a) Annex XI technical documentation and the Article 53(1)(b) downstream-provider information under Annex XII fall away for models under a free and open-source licence with publicly available weights, architecture and usage information, and that carve-out is lost once the model is designated as a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk.

question: What new obligations does that flip impose on us?
answer: All provider obligations transfer. Under Article 25(1), a deployer that makes a substantial modification to a high-risk AI system already placed on the market, or that modifies the intended purpose of a system so that it becomes high-risk, is considered to be the provider and is subject to the provider obligations under Article 16, which require ensuring the system complies with the requirements of Chapter III, Section 2. The initial provider is not released: Article 25(2) obliges it to make available the necessary information and to provide the reasonably expected technical access and other assistance so that the new provider can meet those obligations, in particular the conformity assessment of the high-risk AI system. Article 25(4) additionally requires the necessary information, capabilities, technical access and other assistance from third-party suppliers of AI systems, tools, services, components or processes integrated into the high-risk AI system to be specified in a written agreement, except where such elements, other than general-purpose AI models, are made publicly available under a free and open-source licence.

question: But we built it, so are we provider or deployer? We're both.
answer: Both, and the two roles apply cumulatively. An organisation that develops an AI system and puts it into service under its own name for its own internal use is the provider of that system, and it is simultaneously the deployer because it uses the system under its own authority. Putting the system into service for an Annex III employment, workers' management and access to self-employment use-case, such as recruitment or selection, or decisions on promotion, termination, task allocation and performance monitoring, makes it high-risk under Article 6(2), which classifies Annex III use-cases as high-risk unless an Article 6(3) derogation applies for a narrow procedural task, improving a previously completed human activity, detecting decision-making patterns without replacing human assessment, or a preparatory task, and never where the system performs profiling of natural persons. Where that derogation is relied on, the provider must document the assessment before the system is put into service under Article 6(4).

question: Now we're rebranding it under our own name before selling it on.
answer: Yes, rebranding transfers provider status to the rebranding entity. Article 25 treats any distributor, importer, deployer or other third party as the provider, subject to the provider obligations, where it puts its name or trademark on a high-risk AI system already placed on the market or put into service, without prejudice to contractual arrangements allocating those obligations otherwise, and the initial provider then ceases to be the provider while remaining bound to cooperate closely and supply the necessary information and reasonably expected technical access. For this limited risk system, the rebranding entity assumes the provider transparency duties in Article 50, meaning the system must be designed so that natural persons are informed they are interacting with an AI system unless that is obvious to a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person, with that information given clearly and distinguishably at the latest at the time of first interaction, and any synthetic audio, image, video or text output must be marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated. It must also ensure a sufficient level of AI literacy among its staff and other persons dealing with the operation and use of the system on its behalf (Article 4).

question: What if we keep training and hit 1×10²⁵?
answer: No, the entity's own status is unchanged: it remains the provider within the meaning of Article 3(3), and what shifts is the classification of the model itself. Under Article 51(2) a general-purpose AI model is presumed to have high impact capabilities, and so falls to be classified as a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk under Article 51(1)(a), only where the cumulative training compute is greater than 10^25 floating point operations, so a figure sitting exactly at 1×10^25 does not of itself trigger that presumption, and the July 2025 Commission Guidelines read the same threshold, their separate 10^23 FLOPs presumption going only to whether the model is general-purpose at all. Independently of compute, the Commission may still designate the model as systemic-risk by decision under Article 51(1)(b) on the Annex XIII criteria of parameter count, dataset size and quality, training compute, input and output modalities, benchmarks and capability evaluations, and reach among business users and registered end-users. Once the threshold is crossed or a designation lands, the four Article 55 obligations attach on top of the Article 53 duties, namely model evaluation with documented adversarial testing, assessment and mitigation of systemic risks at Union level, reporting of serious incidents to the AI Office without undue delay, and adequate cybersecurity for the model and its physical infrastructure.

question: Our fine-tune used 3.3×10²⁴ FLOPs — exactly the 1/3 threshold. Are we now a provider?
answer: Not on the compute figure alone. The Act does not specify a one third of training compute threshold that converts a fine-tuner into a provider; instead, Article 25 on responsibilities along the AI value chain provides that a distributor, importer, deployer or other third party is considered the provider, and assumes the provider obligations, where it puts its name or trademark on a high-risk AI system already placed on the market, makes a substantial modification to such a system so that it remains high-risk, or modifies the intended purpose of an AI system, including a general-purpose AI system, so that it becomes high-risk. Where one of those circumstances occurs, the initial provider ceases to be the provider of that specific system and must cooperate closely with the new provider, making available the necessary information and reasonably expected technical access, unless it had clearly specified that its system was not to be changed into a high-risk AI system. Training compute is legally relevant in a different place, as one of the Annex XIII criteria for designating a general-purpose AI model as presenting systemic risk, alongside parameter count, dataset quality and size, input and output modalities, benchmarks and capability evaluations, and reach among business users and registered end-users.

question: We also train it on 2×10²⁵ FLOPs.
answer: At 2×10^25 FLOPs the model is presumed to have high impact capabilities and is therefore classified as a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk under Article 51, which sets that presumption at cumulative training compute above 10^25 floating point operations. That designation removes the Article 53(2) free and open-source exception entirely, so the Apache 2.0 release on HuggingFace no longer excuses the Article 53(1)(a) technical documentation per Annex XI covering architecture, training process, data, compute and evaluation results, nor the Article 53(1)(b) downstream-provider information per Annex XII, and the Article 53(1)(c) copyright policy and Article 53(1)(d) public training-data summary continue to apply as they do to every provider. Article 55 then adds four further obligations: model evaluation including documented adversarial testing under standardised protocols, assessment and mitigation of systemic risks at Union level, tracking and reporting serious incidents and corrective measures to the AI Office without undue delay, and adequate cybersecurity protection for the model and its physical infrastructure. Compliance with those Article 55 duties may be demonstrated through an Article 56 code of practice until a harmonised standard is published, failing which alternative adequate means must be shown to the Commission.

question: Which one wins if my chatbot is also a high-risk medical-triage tool?
answer: Neither wins; both apply cumulatively. Article 50(6) states that the Article 50 transparency duties do not affect the requirements and obligations set out in Chapter III, so the Article 50(1) duty on providers to design AI systems that interact directly with natural persons so those persons are informed they are interacting with an AI system sits alongside the Article 13 duty to make the high-risk system sufficiently transparent for deployers to interpret its output and use it appropriately, with instructions for use covering intended purpose, accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity levels, foreseeable circumstances leading to risks to health, safety or fundamental rights, and human oversight measures. The Article 50(1) disclosure is owed to the natural person and must be given in a clear and distinguishable manner at the latest at the time of the first interaction, in conformity with applicable accessibility requirements (Article 50(5)), while the Article 13 information is owed to the deployer. The only relief from Article 50(1) is where the AI nature is obvious to a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person, or for systems authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences, neither of which fits a triage chatbot addressed to consumers.

question: Does our priority sandbox access carry over?
answer: Not as a matter of entitlement, because Article 62(1)(a) confers priority access to the AI regulatory sandboxes specifically on SMEs, including start-ups, having a registered office or a branch in the Union, and only to the extent that they fulfil the eligibility conditions and selection criteria. What is lost on ceasing to be an SME is the priority ranking, not sandbox participation as such. Participation remains available under Article 57, which obliges each Member State to ensure at least one national AI regulatory sandbox operational by 2 August 2026, offering a controlled environment for the development, training, testing and validation of innovative AI systems for a limited time before placing on the market or putting into service, under a sandbox plan agreed with the competent authority and subject to that authority's guidance and supervision.

question: We sell it to call centres for monitoring agent stress levels.
answer: Prohibited. A call centre is a workplace, so Article 5(1)(f) bans the placing on the market, the putting into service for this specific purpose, and the use of AI systems to infer emotions of a natural person in the areas of workplace and education institutions, and that prohibition binds the provider selling the system for that purpose as well as the call centre deploying it. The only escape is the narrow exception in the same provision for systems intended to be put in place or into the market for medical or safety reasons, which requires that medical or safety purpose to be the system's intended purpose at market placement rather than a label applied afterwards, and generalised monitoring of agent stress for productivity or wellbeing management does not meet it. Emotion recognition remains lawful outside workplace and education institutions, subject to the Article 50 transparency duty on deployers to inform the natural persons exposed to the operation of an emotion recognition system.

question: What if we add ethnicity inference for marketing personalisation?
answer: No. Article 5 prohibits the placing on the market, putting into service or use of biometric categorisation systems that categorise individually natural persons based on their biometric data to deduce or infer their race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation, and inferring ethnicity for marketing personalisation falls squarely within that prohibited practice on race. The only carve-out is the labelling or filtering of lawfully acquired biometric datasets based on biometric data, or the categorising of biometric data in the area of law enforcement, neither of which covers retail marketing personalisation. Age range categorisation is not caught by that prohibition, but biometric categorisation according to sensitive or protected attributes based on the inference of those attributes is a high-risk use case under Annex III, so the age categorisation feature must be assessed against that classification.

question: Do we still need judicial pre-authorization?
answer: Yes. Real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for the purposes of law enforcement is a prohibited practice under Article 5, and the targeted search for missing persons in Article 5(1)(h)(i) is one of only three exhaustive objectives that lift the prohibition, each subject to strict necessity and to prior authorisation granted by a judicial authority or an independent administrative authority of the Member State concerned. In a duly justified situation of urgency the use may begin before authorisation, but authorisation must be requested without undue delay and at the latest within 24 hours, and if it is refused the use must stop immediately with the data deleted. Article 5 also leaves the exception dependent on national law, so a police force may rely on it only where the Member State has enabled that objective in national law, which may impose stricter conditions than the Regulation.

question: Now we use it to decide who to lay off in a restructuring.
answer: High-risk. An AI system used to evaluate the performance of persons in work-related relationships and to inform termination decisions falls squarely within the employment, workers' management and access to self-employment use case in Annex III(4)(b), which covers systems intended to make decisions affecting terms of work-related relationships, including the promotion or termination of work-related contractual relationships, and to monitor and evaluate the performance and behaviour of such persons. Article 6(2) classifies any system listed in Annex III as high-risk. The Article 6(3) derogation for systems posing no significant risk of harm, limited to a narrow procedural task, improving the result of a previously completed human activity, detecting decision-making patterns without replacing or influencing the human assessment, or a preparatory task, is unavailable where the system materially influences layoff outcomes, and it never applies where the system performs profiling of natural persons.

question: We want to deploy it to a real client during the sandbox phase.
answer: No, not as a commercial deployment. An AI regulatory sandbox under Article 57 provides only a controlled environment for development, training, testing and validation for a limited time before the system is placed on the market or put into service, pursuant to the specific sandbox plan agreed with the competent authority, and it may include testing in real world conditions supervised within the sandbox under Article 57(5), so any involvement of a real client must fall within that agreed plan and remain supervised testing rather than live provision of the service. Where testing with a real client is to occur outside the sandbox, Article 60 permits it before placing on the market only if a real-world testing plan is submitted to and approved by the market surveillance authority of the Member State concerned, the testing is registered with a Union-wide unique single identification number, informed consent is obtained from subjects who may withdraw at any time, the provider or prospective provider is established in the Union or has an Union legal representative, and serious incidents are reported under Article 73 with immediate mitigation, suspension or termination. Liability for damage remains with the provider or prospective provider in both settings under Articles 57(12) and 60(9), although no administrative fines are imposed for infringements of this Regulation where the sandbox plan, its terms and conditions, and the competent authority's guidance are observed in good faith, and the authority retains the power to suspend the testing or the sandbox participation where significant risks to health, safety or fundamental rights cannot be effectively mitigated.

question: We're a 25-employee startup — does the €35M cap actually hit us?
answer: No, not as an absolute figure: for SMEs and start-ups Article 99(6) reverses the ordinary rule in Article 99(3), so the applicable ceiling for an Article 5 prohibited practice is the lower of EUR 35 000 000 or 7 % of total worldwide annual turnover, rather than whichever is higher. For a 25-employee undertaking that means the effective maximum is 7 % of total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, since that figure will fall far below the fixed amount. The exposure is a reduced ceiling, not an exemption, and Article 99 further requires that any fine be effective, proportionate and dissuasive and proportionate to the gravity and nature of the infringement, which allows the knowing six-month duration of the Article 5 breach to weigh against the undertaking. Article 5 places prohibited practices outside any conformity or remediation pathway, so the only mitigation available is immediate cessation and cooperation, not retrospective compliance.

question: We're under Annex III(4) (employment). Which route?
answer: The Annex III route under Article 6(2), which classifies a system as high-risk because it falls within a listed use case rather than because it is a safety component of a product under Annex I harmonisation legislation subject to third-party conformity assessment (Article 6(1)). Within point 4 of Annex III on employment, workers' management and access to self-employment, the two lettered use cases are recruitment or selection of natural persons, in particular placing targeted job advertisements, analysing and filtering job applications and evaluating candidates, and decisions affecting terms of work-related relationships, promotion or termination of such contractual relationships, allocation of tasks based on individual behaviour or personal traits or characteristics, and monitoring and evaluating performance and behaviour of persons in such relationships. The system is high-risk only where it matches one of those lettered use cases, since the numbered heading alone does not classify it. Article 6(3) removes it from high-risk where it poses no significant risk of harm and performs a narrow procedural task, improves the result of a previously completed human activity, detects decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the previously completed human assessment, or performs a preparatory task, unless it performs profiling of natural persons, in which case it is always high-risk, and the provider must document that assessment before placing the system on the market or putting it into service.

question: And for Annex I (medical devices etc.) embedded systems?
answer: Annex I embedded systems apply later, from 2 August 2027. Article 113(3)(c) defers Article 6(1) and the corresponding obligations to that date, separately from the Regulation's general application on 2 August 2026. Article 6(1) classifies an AI system as high-risk where it is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, which includes Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on medical devices and Regulation (EU) 2017/746 on in vitro diagnostic medical devices, and only where that product must undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that sectoral legislation.

question: Did the Digital Omnibus push that back?
answer: No. The Regulation as enacted contains no deferral of that kind, and its own text does not provide for any postponement of the high-risk regime by a later legislative package. The classification route in Article 6(2), under which an AI system is high-risk where it falls within one of the listed use-cases under the eight areas of Annex III, therefore continues to apply as enacted, together with the accompanying Chapter III duties such as the Article 13 requirement that a high-risk AI system be sufficiently transparent for deployers to interpret its output and be accompanied by instructions for use. Any change to those application dates would have to come from an amending act, and until such an act enters into force the timetable in the Regulation governs.

question: If we don't sign, what's the alternative path to demonstrate compliance?
answer: Signing the Code of Practice is voluntary, and a provider that does not adhere to it must instead demonstrate alternative adequate means of compliance for assessment by the Commission under Article 53(4), or comply with a European harmonised standard once published, which grants a presumption of conformity to the extent the standard covers the obligations. The substantive duties are unchanged either way: under Article 53(1) the provider must draw up and keep up to date technical documentation per Annex XI, make available to downstream providers the information set out in Annex XII, put in place a policy to comply with Union law on copyright, and publish a sufficiently detailed summary of the content used for training. Where the model is classified as a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk under Article 51, the same alternative-means route applies under Article 55(2) to the additional duties of model evaluation including adversarial testing, systemic-risk assessment and mitigation, serious-incident reporting to the AI Office, and adequate cybersecurity protection for the model and its physical infrastructure. Any documentation submitted, including trade secrets, is handled under the confidentiality obligations referred to in Article 55(3).

question: Can they fine us directly?
answer: No. The AI Office does not itself impose fines on providers of general-purpose AI models, because that penalty decision power rests with the Commission, which the AI Office serves as operational support. Article 53 casts the AI Office in a supervisory and information-receiving role, since under Article 53(1)(a) the Annex XI technical documentation on the model's training, testing and evaluation is provided to the AI Office and national competent authorities upon request, and under Article 53(1)(d) the publicly available summary of training content follows a template provided by the AI Office. The enforcement counterpart sits with the Commission, as Article 53(3) obliges providers to cooperate with the Commission and the national competent authorities in the exercise of their powers, and Article 53(4) requires a provider that neither adheres to an approved code of practice nor complies with a harmonised standard to demonstrate alternative adequate means of compliance for assessment by the Commission. For a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk, Article 55(1)(c) likewise routes reporting of serious incidents and possible corrective measures to the AI Office without conferring on it any power to levy penalties.

question: Do we have to retrofit conformity, or are we grandfathered?
answer: Grandfathered, but only conditionally. Article 111, which sets the transitional regime for AI systems already placed on the market, provides that the Regulation applies to operators of high-risk AI systems placed on the market or put into service before 2 August 2026 only if, as from that date, those systems are subject to significant changes in their designs, so a March 2026 placement escapes retrofit for as long as the design remains materially unchanged. Where the high-risk AI system is intended to be used by public authorities, that relief is limited: the provider and the deployer must in any case take the necessary steps to comply with the requirements and obligations of the Regulation by 2 August 2030. A separate and later date applies only to AI systems that are components of the large-scale IT systems established by the acts listed in Annex X, being the Schengen Information System, the Visa Information System, Eurodac, the Entry/Exit System, the European Travel Information and Authorisation System, ECRIS-TCN and the interoperability Regulations, which must be brought into compliance by 31 December 2030.

question: A customer wants to know why their loan was rejected by our AI.
answer: Yes, an affected person subject to a loan denial is entitled to be given the reasons for that decision, and the deployer must be in a position to supply them. Article 13 requires the high-risk AI system to be sufficiently transparent for the deployer to interpret its output and to be accompanied by instructions for use covering the system's capabilities and limitations and the foreseeable circumstances that may lead to risks to fundamental rights, so the deployer holds the information needed to explain a rejection. Article 27(1) obliges a deployer of an Annex III point 5(b) creditworthiness or credit scoring system to carry out a fundamental rights impact assessment before first use, covering the categories of persons affected, the specific risks of harm, the human oversight measures applied and the internal governance and complaint mechanisms through which an affected person can contest the outcome. Article 26 supports that entitlement in operation by requiring use of the system in accordance with the instructions for use, human oversight assigned to natural persons with the necessary competence, training and authority, and retention of the automatically generated logs for at least six months, although a deployer that is a financial institution subject to Union financial services internal governance requirements satisfies the monitoring and log retention duties by complying with those governance arrangements.

question: If the US parent has no EU establishment, who plays the authorized-representative role?
answer: The US parent, as a provider established in a third country, must appoint by written mandate an authorised representative established in the Union prior to making the high-risk AI system available on the Union market, and the absence of any EU establishment does not remove that duty but is precisely what triggers it (Article 22). The mandate empowers that representative to verify that the EU declaration of conformity and the technical documentation have been drawn up and that an appropriate conformity assessment was carried out, to keep those documents and the provider's contact details at the disposal of authorities for ten years, to supply information and log access on reasoned request, to cooperate with competent authorities, and to comply with the registration obligations, and it allows the authorities to address the representative in addition to or instead of the provider (Article 22). Any EU affiliate may be appointed to that role, but appointment does not transfer the provider's own obligations, and an affiliate that merely makes the system available on the market remains separately bound as a distributor to verify the CE marking, the EU declaration of conformity and the instructions for use (Article 24). The authorised representative must terminate the mandate and inform the relevant market surveillance authority if it has reason to consider the provider to be acting contrary to the Regulation (Article 22).

question: Is an AI spam filter regulated under the AI Act?
answer: An AI spam filter is minimal-risk and therefore not subject to substantive obligations under the AI Act, being neither a prohibited practice under Article 5 nor high-risk under either route of Article 6. It is not high-risk because it is not a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, and filtering unsolicited messages does not fall within any of the eight high-risk areas enumerated in Annex III. The Article 50 transparency obligations, which require providers to ensure that AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons disclose their AI nature and that synthetic content is marked in a machine-readable format, are likewise not engaged by a system that merely classifies incoming messages rather than interacting with or generating content for natural persons. Classification would change only where such a system were deployed for a listed Annex III use case, for example to analyse and filter job applications in the employment area.

question: Is an AI inventory-management tool high-risk under the AI Act?
answer: An AI inventory-management tool is not high-risk in ordinary commercial use, and it is not among the practices prohibited under Article 5. Under Article 6 it becomes high-risk only on one of two routes: where it is a safety component of a product, or is itself a product, covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and that product must undergo a third-party conformity assessment (Article 6(1)), or where it falls within one of the use cases listed in Annex III (Article 6(2)), such as inventory functions embedded in the management or operation of critical infrastructure. Absent either route, the system is minimal risk, subject only to the Article 50 transparency obligation that natural persons be informed they are interacting with an AI system where the tool interacts with them directly and this is not obvious. Classification therefore turns on the deployment context rather than on the inventory function itself.

question: Is an AI opponent in a video game regulated under the AI Act?
answer: An AI opponent in a video game is minimal risk and subject to no substantive obligations under the Regulation. It is not among the practices prohibited by Article 5, which bans subliminal, manipulative or deceptive techniques causing significant harm and the exploitation of vulnerabilities by age, disability or socio-economic situation, a game adversary calibrating difficulty does not meet that threshold absent an intent or effect of materially distorting behaviour to a person's significant detriment. It is likewise not high-risk under Article 6, since it is neither a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I nor within any of the eight areas listed in Annex III. Where the system interacts directly with natural persons through conversational dialogue or generates synthetic audio, image, video or text content, the provider remains bound by the Article 50 transparency obligations to disclose the system's artificial nature at the latest at the time of first interaction and to mark such outputs in a machine-readable, detectable format.

question: Is a music recommendation AI high-risk under the AI Act?
answer: A music recommendation AI is not high-risk. It is neither a safety component of, nor itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I requiring third-party conformity assessment under Article 6(1), nor does it fall within any of the Annex III use cases that Article 6(2) designates as high-risk, and it does not engage any prohibited practice under Article 5, which bans only exhaustively listed practices such as subliminal, manipulative or deceptive techniques causing significant harm and exploitation of vulnerabilities by age, disability or socio-economic situation. It is therefore a minimal-risk system, subject only to the Article 50 transparency obligation where it interacts directly with natural persons, requiring those persons to be informed that they are interacting with an AI system unless that is obvious to a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person, with that information given clearly at the latest at the time of first interaction. A recommender system would become high-risk only if its intended purpose were repurposed into an Annex III use case.

question: Is a customer service chatbot high-risk under the AI Act?
answer: A customer service chatbot is not high-risk, unless it is deployed within one of the Annex III use cases, such as evaluating eligibility for essential public assistance benefits and services, assessing creditworthiness, or evaluating and classifying emergency calls. It is not a prohibited practice under Article 5, which exhaustively bans manipulative or deceptive techniques, exploitation of vulnerabilities, social scoring, criminal-offence risk assessment based solely on profiling, and the other listed practices, none of which describe ordinary customer support. Outside those Annex III use cases and absent its use as a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation in Annex I requiring third-party conformity assessment under Article 6(1), the system falls in the limited risk tier. In that case the provider must ensure, under Article 50, that the chatbot is designed so natural persons are informed they are interacting with an AI system unless this is obvious to a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person, with that information given clearly and distinguishably at the latest at the time of the first interaction.

question: Is a translation AI high-risk under the AI Act?
answer: A translation AI system is not high-risk unless it is intended to be used as a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and that product must undergo third-party conformity assessment (Article 6(1)), or its intended purpose falls within one of the Annex III use cases such as translation deployed by law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control authorities or in education or employment decision-making (Article 6(2)). General-purpose translation for communication, content localisation or consumer use satisfies neither route and is therefore limited risk or minimal risk. Where such a system interacts directly with natural persons, the provider must ensure they are informed that they are interacting with an AI system unless this is obvious to a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person, and synthetic AI-generated content must be marked in a machine-readable, detectable format (Article 50).

question: Is an AI image generator high-risk under the AI Act?
answer: An AI image generator is not high-risk in itself, and is high-risk only where it is used as a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment under Article 6(1), or where it is put into service for one of the Annex III use cases pursuant to Article 6(2). Generating synthetic images is not among the AI practices prohibited under Article 5, which bans subliminal, purposefully manipulative or deceptive techniques and the exploitation of vulnerabilities due to age, disability or a specific social or economic situation where these materially distort behaviour and cause or are reasonably likely to cause significant harm. Absent either high-risk route, the system is limited risk, and the provider must under Article 50 ensure that its outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated, effectively, interoperably, robustly and reliably as far as technically feasible. That marking duty does not apply to the extent the system performs an assistive function for standard editing or does not substantially alter the input data provided by the deployer or the semantics thereof, or where authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences.

question: Are subliminal or manipulative AI techniques prohibited?
answer: Prohibited, but only where the technique meets the harm threshold: Article 5(1)(a) bans placing on the market, putting into service or use of an AI system deploying subliminal techniques beyond a person's consciousness or purposefully manipulative or deceptive techniques with the objective or effect of materially distorting behaviour by appreciably impairing the ability to make an informed decision, thereby causing a decision that would not otherwise have been taken, in a manner that causes or is reasonably likely to cause significant harm to that person, another person or a group. Article 5(1)(b) separately prohibits AI systems exploiting vulnerabilities due to age, disability or a specific social or economic situation with the same distortion objective or effect and the same significant harm threshold. Because material distortion and significant harm are cumulative conditions, persuasive techniques that do not appreciably impair informed decision-making or do not cause or risk significant harm fall outside the prohibition. Article 5(8) preserves prohibitions arising where such a practice infringes other Union law.

question: Are deceptive or manipulative AI systems prohibited under the AI Act?
answer: Prohibited, but only where the deceptive or manipulative character meets the full threshold of Article 5(1)(a), which bars placing on the market, putting into service or use of an AI system deploying subliminal techniques beyond a person's consciousness or purposefully manipulative or deceptive techniques with the objective or effect of materially distorting behaviour by appreciably impairing the ability to make an informed decision, thereby causing a decision that would not otherwise have been taken, in a manner that causes or is reasonably likely to cause significant harm. Manipulative or deceptive techniques that do not appreciably impair informed decision-making or that carry no reasonable likelihood of significant harm, ordinary persuasive advertising, for instance, fall outside that prohibition. A closely related prohibition in Article 5(1)(b) covers AI systems exploiting vulnerabilities due to age, disability or a specific social or economic situation with the objective or effect of materially distorting behaviour in a manner causing or reasonably likely to cause significant harm, and there the impairment of informed decision-making need not be shown. Article 5 does not affect prohibitions applying where an AI practice infringes other Union law.

question: Is untargeted scraping or harvesting of facial images prohibited?
answer: Yes, prohibited. Article 5 prohibits the placing on the market, the putting into service for this specific purpose, or the use of AI systems that create or expand facial recognition databases through the untargeted scraping of facial images from the internet or CCTV footage. The prohibition attaches to the untargeted character of the collection, so it applies irrespective of whether the resulting database is temporary, centralised or decentralised, and Article 5 further provides that it does not affect prohibitions arising where the practice infringes other Union law. Targeted searching for a specific identified individual does not create or expand a facial recognition database through untargeted scraping and therefore falls outside this prohibition.

question: Is a recruitment or hiring AI high-risk under the AI Act?
answer: Recruitment and hiring AI is high-risk, by virtue of Article 6(2), which classifies as high-risk any AI system falling within the use cases listed in Annex III, among them employment, workers management and access to self-employment. That heading covers AI systems intended to be used for the recruitment or selection of natural persons, in particular to place targeted job advertisements, to analyse and filter job applications, and to evaluate candidates, as well as systems used to make decisions on promotion, termination, task allocation, and monitoring or evaluation of performance and behaviour. Such a system is not a prohibited practice under Article 5, whose bans are exhaustive and do not extend to employment screening, so it sits in the high-risk tier rather than the prohibited tier. Where the system also interacts directly with candidates, the Article 50 transparency obligation applies in addition, requiring the provider to ensure that natural persons are informed they are interacting with an AI system unless that is obvious, in a clear and distinguishable manner at the latest at the time of first interaction.

question: Is social scoring prohibited or high-risk under the AI Act?
answer: Social scoring is prohibited, not high-risk, under Article 5(1)(c), which bans placing on the market, putting into service or use of AI systems that evaluate or classify natural persons or groups over a certain period of time on the basis of their social behaviour or known, inferred or predicted personal or personality characteristics. The prohibition bites where the social score leads to detrimental or unfavourable treatment in social contexts unrelated to those in which the data was originally generated or collected, or to detrimental or unfavourable treatment that is unjustified or disproportionate to the social behaviour or its gravity. It applies to any provider or deployer, public or private, and is not conditioned on the sector of deployment. Absent either of those two detrimental-treatment limbs, an evaluation or scoring system falls outside the Article 5 prohibition and must instead be assessed under the ordinary classification rules.

question: What transparency obligations apply to a provider of a high-risk AI system under Articles 13 and 50?
answer: A provider of a high-risk AI system carries transparency duties on two separate tracks, one owed to deployers and one owed to natural persons. Article 13 requires that the system be designed and developed so that its operation is sufficiently transparent to enable deployers to interpret its output and use it appropriately, and that it be accompanied by instructions for use containing concise, complete, correct and clear information covering the provider's identity and contact details and, where applicable, those of its authorised representative, the characteristics, capabilities and limitations of performance (intended purpose, the level of accuracy including its metrics, robustness and cybersecurity, known or foreseeable circumstances that may lead to risks to health and safety or fundamental rights, the technical capabilities to explain the output, performance regarding specific persons or groups, input data and training, validation and testing data specifications, and information enabling deployers to interpret the output), any pre-determined changes, the human oversight measures, the computational and hardware resources, expected lifetime and necessary maintenance and care measures, and the mechanisms allowing deployers to collect, store and interpret the logs. Article 50 adds two obligations that fall on the provider itself: systems intended to interact directly with natural persons must be designed so those persons are informed they are interacting with an AI system, unless that is obvious to a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person, and the duty does not apply to systems authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences unless they are available for the public to report an offence; and systems generating synthetic audio, image, video or text content must mark their outputs in a machine-readable format detectable as artificially generated or manipulated, using solutions that are effective, interoperable, robust and reliable as far as technically feasible, save where the system performs an assistive function for standard editing or does not substantially alter the deployer's input data or its semantics.
